evidence.claim: Many of Ipswich’s First Period houses remain occupied, part of the country’s largest surviving collection.
evidence.quote: Many First Period houses are still standing and occupied today – more than any other community in the country.

evidence.claim: The byway passes roughly 59 of these early homes.
evidence.quote: Drive past the largest collection (roughly 59 homes) of remaining First Period houses in the country.

evidence.claim: Their survival has an economic history: nineteenth-century clipper ships favored deeper ports, and residents stayed in older houses they could not afford to replace.
evidence.quote: Great clipper ships of the 19th century bypassed Ipswich in favor of the deep-water seaports at Salem, Newburyport, Quincy, and Boston. The town remained primarily a fishing and farming community, its residents living in older homes they could not afford to replace—leaving Ipswich with a considerable inventory of early architecture.

evidence.claim: The river also powered mills, and salt marshes supplied livestock with hay.
evidence.quote: The tidal Ipswich River provided water power for mills, and salt marshes supplied hay for livestock.

evidence.claim: The drive through downtown follows parts of that working river, with the early houses remaining in the townscape.
evidence.quote: The Coastal Byway brings you through downtown Ipswich and along parts of the scenic Ipswich River. Drive past the largest collection (roughly 59 homes) of remaining First Period houses in the country.

evidence.claim: By the mid-eighteenth century, wharves and storehouses lined the river alongside tanning and shipbuilding operations.
evidence.quote: By the mid-1700s, wharfs and storehouses lined the Ipswich River shores along with salt watchers, tannery, and shipbuilding operations.

evidence.claim: Essex’s center lies on marshland beside the Essex River, within the Great Marsh.
evidence.quote: The central part of Essex lies on marshland surrounding the Essex River. This is a portion of the larger Great Marsh

evidence.claim: Its shipyards supplied schooners to Gloucester and other Atlantic fishing communities.

evidence.claim: The industry failed to adapt to the change from wooden sailing ships to metal vessels driven by engines and disappeared around World War II.
evidence.quote: Essex did not adapt to the transition from sail-powered wooden ships to engine-powered metal vessels, and this activity disappeared around World War II.

evidence.claim: Wooden boatbuilding continues on a smaller scale: beside the Essex Shipbuilding Museum, the Story Family’s yard constructs and launches wooden ships.
evidence.quote: Adjacent to the museum is a boat yard owned by the Story Family, which still constructs and launches wooden ships built in the Essex tradition.

evidence.claim: The Man at the Wheel looks out over Gloucester Harbor from a base of sea-green granite.
evidence.quote: The monument has a square base of sea green granite. It is positioned so that the fisherman is looking out over Gloucester Harbor.

evidence.claim: The eight-foot bronze fisherman wears oilskins and braces at the wheel on a sloping deck.
evidence.quote: It is an 8-foot-tall (2.4 m), bronze statue of a fisherman dressed in oilskins standing braced at the wheel on the sloping deck of his ship.

evidence.claim: Leonard Craske designed the sculpture, which the Gorham Company cast in 1925.
evidence.quote: The English sculptor Leonard Craske (1882–1950) designed the sculpture, and it was cast by the Gorham Company of Providence, Rhode Island, in 1925.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service describes its purpose as commemorating Gloucester’s 300th anniversary and the thousands of fishermen lost at sea during those centuries.
evidence.quote: The Gloucester Tercentenary Permanent Memorial Association sponsored an artistic competition to commemorate Gloucester's 300th anniversary and to permanently memorialize the thousands of fishermen lost at sea in the first three centuries of Gloucester's history.

evidence.claim: On the harbor-facing panel, bronze lettering quotes Psalm 107:23.
evidence.quote: A larger recessed panel on the front or harbor-facing side of the base holds an inscription of bronze letters taken from the Bible's Psalm 107:23

evidence.claim: The inscription reads “They That Go Down To The Sea In Ships 1623-1923,” placing three centuries beneath the figure.
